title: Salvador Luria, a Jewish refugee from Italy, showed with Max Delbrück that mutations in bacteria occur at random

trailer.text: Salvador Luria was an Italian-American biologist who in 1969 won the Nobel Prize for Physiology or Medicine, together with Max Delbrück and Alfred Hershey.
He was born in 1912 to a Jewish family in Turin.
According to MIT Technology Review, race laws barred him from a research fellowship in Italy, so he left for Paris in 1938.
In 1943 Luria and Delbrück published an analysis of mutations in E. coli bacteria that confer resistance to bacterial viruses.
They concluded that the resistance resulted from spontaneous mutations, independent of exposure to the virus.

stations.title: From Turin to New York Harbor

paragraphs.text: He was the second son of a lower-middle-class Jewish family.
In July 1938 Mussolini passed race laws that restricted the participation of Jews in public life.
According to MIT Technology Review, the laws barred Luria from a research fellowship, so he left for Paris in 1938.
When the German army invaded in June 1940, Luria traveled by bicycle to Marseilles to obtain an American visa.
On 12 September 1940 he entered New York Harbor with $52 and the clothes on his back.
According to his autobiography, he was better off than many of the other 800 refugees on the ship.
In New York, with Fermi's help, he received a Rockefeller Foundation fellowship and worked at the College of Physicians and Surgeons at Columbia University.
On his application for citizenship he changed his first name from Salvatore to Salvador and added a middle name, Edward.

stations.title: An open question, and a meeting with Delbrück

paragraphs.text: Some scientists believed that the interaction between bacteriophages, viruses that attack bacteria, and the bacteria themselves could induce resistance in the bacteria.
Luria wrote in a 1947 review that bacteriology had been one of the last strongholds of Lamarckism.
The question lay between two hypotheses.
According to one, the viruses directly cause resistance in the bacteria.
According to the other, the resistance depends on a pre-existing genetic change, and the viruses only select the resistant bacteria.
In December 1940 Luria met Max Delbrück.
At the end of 1941 Luria worked with Thomas Anderson, and was among the first to photograph bacteriophages with an electron microscope and accurately measure their size.
Luria realized that mutations in bacteria could be seen as analogous to jackpot wins.
According to Live Science, he realized that statistics could be used to distinguish between random mutations and mutations induced by the phages.

According to the Genetics article, a mutation in an early generation, in a culture of 10 doublings, would yield up to 1,024 resistant cells at the end of the culture, and this effect is called a "jackpot".
In January 1943 Luria moved to Bloomington, Indiana, to teach at Indiana University.
According to Live Science, they exposed the bacteria to phages and serially cultured them on plates.
In eight small parallel cultures, the variance (corrected for sampling) in the number of resistant bacteria ranged from 40.8 to 3,498, according to Table 2 in their paper.
In three experiments of 10 samples from one large culture, the variance was much lower: 15, 27 and 3.8.
Luria and Delbrück concluded that resistance to T1 phage in the E. coli B strain resulted from spontaneous mutations, independent of exposure to the virus.
In 1943 Luria, then at Indiana University, and Delbrück, then at Vanderbilt, published the analysis.
According to the Nobel website, Luria and Delbrück proved through statistical investigations that bacteria, like more complex organisms, develop via mutations.
According to the National Library of Medicine, the work provided statistical evidence for the existence of genes in bacteria, and established microbes as suitable subjects for genetics research.
According to the Genetics article, the study helped develop the concept of random mutation.
The historian Thomas Brock identifies the 1943 paper as the founding document of modern bacterial genetics.
According to MIT Technology Review, the work of Luria, Delbrück and Hershey led to an explosion in bacterial genetics research.
According to Andrew Murray, the paper showed that elegant statistical analysis could illuminate biological processes that cannot be directly observed.
Delbrück and Luria introduced genetic concepts and rigorous quantitative methods into bacteriophage research.
Around the three, a "phage group" informally grew up, with its center at the Biological Laboratory in Cold Spring Harbor.

stations.title: A broken tube, and a textbook

paragraphs.text: Luria was the first to discover the restriction-modification phenomenon, in which bacteria protect themselves by altering the DNA of invading phages.
In the 1960s other researchers discovered that the changes were the result of bacterial restriction enzymes, which degraded viral DNA as a defense mechanism.
In 1953 Luria published General Virology, the first comprehensive textbook in the field.
In 1969 Luria won the Nobel Prize for Physiology or Medicine, together with Max Delbrück and Alfred Hershey.
The prize was awarded for their discoveries concerning the replication mechanism and the genetic structure of viruses.
According to the committee, the three set the foundations on which modern molecular biology rests.

In October 1969, the day after the Moratorium march against the Vietnam War in Boston on 15 October, Luria's Nobel Prize was announced, and he declared that he would donate part of the prize money to the peace movement.
Luria also won the Lenghi Prize of the Accademia dei Lincei in 1965, and Columbia University's Louisa Gross Horwitz Prize in 1969.
His book Life: The Unfinished Experiment won the National Book Award in 1974.
In 1991 he received the National Medal of Science.
Luria's first student was James Watson.
According to MIT Technology Review, Luria mentored Nobel Prize winners such as James Watson, David Baltimore, Susumu Tonegawa and Phillip Sharp.
At MIT Luria was appointed Sedgwick Professor of Biology.
According to MIT Technology Review, in 1972 he led an effort to secure a $4.4 million grant from the National Cancer Institute to establish the MIT Center for Cancer Research.
He directed the center until 1985.
In 1945 Luria married Zella Hurwitz. Their son Daniel was born in 1948 according to the Discovery Encyclopedia, and in 1949 according to the National Library of Medicine.
Luria died in Lexington, Massachusetts, on 6 February 1991.

stations.title: A passport, a blacklist and doubts about the experiment

paragraphs.text: According to the Discovery Encyclopedia, a two-year FBI investigation found no evidence of Communist or subversive activity against Luria, yet he was denied a passport. According to the Discovery Encyclopedia this happened in 1952 (and elsewhere in the same encyclopedia, in 1951), and according to the American Association of Immunologists, in 1953.
According to the American Association of Immunologists, the passport was denied when he sought to travel to give a paper at a scientific meeting in Oxford.
A few days after his Nobel win it emerged that his name was on a blacklist of the National Institutes of Health, which barred him from advising on grants.
According to the National Library of Medicine, he was an outspoken critic of the Israeli invasion of Lebanon and of the American intervention in Vietnam.
According to the Genetics article, the E. coli strain chosen by Luria and Delbrück lacked an operative CRISPR-Cas mechanism, probably by chance.

According to Live Science, recent research indicates that had a different bacterium-phage system been chosen, for example one that uses CRISPR, the statistical results would not have been so clear-cut.
Biomathematicians have since refined the understanding of distributions that describe the mutational process better than the one used by Luria and Delbrück.
A 2017 paper in Phys Biol argues that the experiment does not rule out Lamarckian evolution.
Mechanisms of resistance based on stable changes in transcription, in metabolism or in the acquisition of genetic material from outside were not examined in the 1943 study.

claims.quote: Luria married Zella Hurwitz, a psychologist, in 1945. Their only child, Daniel, was born in 1949.

claims.text: לוריה מת בלקסינגטון, מסצ'וסטס, ב-6 בפברואר 1991 מהתקף לב.
claims.quote: Luria died in Lexington, Massachusetts, on February 6, 1991, of a heart attack.

claims.text: לפי אנציקלופדיה דיסקברי, חקירה בת שנתיים של ה-FBI לא מצאה פעילות קומוניסטית או חתרנית, אך לוריה נשלל ממנו דרכון ב-1952.
claims.quote: A two-year investigation yielded no evidence of Communist or other subversive activity, but Luria was nevertheless denied a passport in 1952.

claims.text: לפי אנציקלופדיה דיסקברי, ב-1951 סורב ללוריה דרכון בגלל אקטיביזם פוליטי.
claims.quote: In 1951 Luria was refused a passport as a result of his outspoken political activism.

claims.text: לפי איגוד האימונולוגים האמריקאי, ב-1953 נשלל מלוריה דרכון לנסוע להרצאה בכנס מדעי באוקספורד.
claims.quote: Luria, in 1953, was denied a passport to deliver a paper at a scientific meeting in Oxford, England.

claims.text: ימים ספורים אחרי הזכייה התברר ששמו של לוריה ברשימה שחורה של המכונים הלאומיים לבריאות שאסרה עליו לייעץ במענקים.
claims.quote: Nixon’s administration had blacklisted him from advising the NIH on scientific grants, apparently because of his vocal role in mobilizing faculty and public sentiment against the Vietnam War.

claims.text: לפי ספריית הרפואה הלאומית, לוריה היה מבקר חריף של הפלישה הישראלית ללבנון ושל ההתערבות האמריקאית בווייטנאם.
claims.quote: He was also an active participant in the peace movement and was an outspoken critic of the Israeli invasion of Lebanon and the American intervention in Vietnam.

claims.text: לפי מאמר Genetics, זן ה-E. coli שבחרו לוריה ודלבריק חסר מנגנון CRISPR-Cas פעיל, כנראה במקרה.
claims.quote: the E. coli strain selected by Luria and Delbrück for their experiments lacked an operative CRISPR-Cas mechanism

claims.text: לפי Live Science, מחקר עדכני מצביע שאילו נבחרה מערכת חיידק-פאג אחרת, כמו כזו שמשתמשת ב-CRISPR, התוצאות הסטטיסטיות לא היו ברורות כל כך.
claims.quote: if the team had chosen a different bacterium and phage system to study — such as one that used the bacterial immune system CRISPR to fight off phages — the statistical results would not have been so clear-cut.

claims.text: ביומתמטיקאים שכללו מאז את ההבנה של התפלגויות מתמטיות שמתארות את תהליך המוטציה טוב יותר מזו שבה השתמשו לוריה ודלבריק.
claims.quote: biomathematicians have refined understanding of mathematical distributions that better describe the mutational process than the one adopted by Luria and Delbrück

claims.text: מאמר ב-Phys Biol (2017) טוען שהניסוי הקלאסי של לוריה ודלבריק אינו שולל אבולוציה למרקיאנית.
claims.quote: Luria-Delbrück, revisited: the classic experiment does not rule out Lamarckian evolution.

claims.text: מנגנוני עמידות המבוססים על שינויים יציבים בתעתוק, בחילוף חומרים או ברכישת חומר גנטי מבחוץ לא נבדקו במחקר מ-1943.
claims.quote: Mechanisms of resistance that depend on relatively stable changes in transcription, metabolism, or acquisition of new genetic material from sources outside the cell all represent pathways not addressed in the study from 1943.

claims.text: לפי בריטניקה, לוריה הפך ב-1974 למנהל מרכז המחקר לסרטן ב-MIT.
claims.quote: In 1974 he became director of the Center for Cancer Research at MIT.
